Create a scientific medical illustration titled "Tumor Grade" showing four circular microscopy panels side by side, labeled Grade 1 through Grade 4, with a horizontal gradient arrow beneath them labeled from left to right: "Well differentiated → Moderately differentiated → Poorly differentiated → Undifferentiated."
All panels should use a hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining color palette: pale pink cytoplasm and purple/violet nuclei on a light pink background.

Grade 1 (Well Differentiated): Cells are elongated and organized in parallel rows, resembling normal tissue architecture. Nuclei are small, uniform, oval-shaped, and evenly spaced. Cell borders are clearly defined. Minimal nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
Grade 2 (Moderately Differentiated): Cells are rounder and less organized than Grade 1, losing the parallel arrangement. Nuclei are slightly larger and more variable in size and shape. Some loss of tissue architecture. Moderate nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
Grade 3 (Poorly Differentiated): Cells are predominantly round, densely packed, with significant loss of normal tissue structure. Nuclei are enlarged, irregular, and hyperchromatic (darker purple staining). High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Prominent nucleoli may be visible.
Grade 4 (Undifferentiated): Cells are highly pleomorphic — highly variable in size and shape. Nuclei are very large, irregular, and intensely hyperchromatic, nearly filling the cell. Extreme nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Complete loss of normal tissue architecture. Some cells may appear multinucleated.

Style: Clean, professional biomedical textbook illustration. Flat vector or digital painting style. White background. Bold sans-serif labels. Circular panels with thin dark borders. Include a right-pointing arrow beneath all four panels spanning the full width."

Chapter 1: The Stochastic Machine — Understanding LLM Output Generation
The Same Question, Three Different Answers
Nik Bear Brown
Mar 16, 2026

Run this prompt through a large language model three times in a single afternoon:

“In one sentence, describe Wonder Woman’s primary superpower.”

At temperature 0, the model responds the same way every time: something about superhuman strength and combat training, reliably, mechanically, with the confidence of a lookup table. At temperature 0.7, the answers begin to drift — one response emphasizes her divine heritage, another her Lasso of Truth, a third her indestructible bracelets. At temperature 1.2, the outputs become genuinely surprising: the model might foreground her diplomatic mission, her empathy as a weapon, or in one documented run, her capacity to inspire others as the superpower that subsumes all others.

Nothing about Wonder Woman changed between those three runs. The model’s weights did not update. The training data did not shift. The only thing that changed was a single scalar parameter — temperature — that governs how the model samples from the probability distribution it has learned over language. The variation you observed is not noise. It is not a bug. It is the intended, designed, mathematically principled behavior of a system that does not retrieve answers. It generates them, probabilistically, every single time.

This chapter is about what that means.

The Probabilistic Generation Pipeline
Before the theory unfolds section by section, it helps to have a map. Every output a language model produces travels through the same sequence of operations:

Tokens→Logits→Temperature Scaling→Softmax→Sampling→Autoregressive Loop\text{Tokens} \rightarrow \text{Logits} \rightarrow \text{Temperature Scaling} \rightarrow \text{Softmax} \rightarrow \text{Sampling} \rightarrow \text{Autoregressive Loop} Tokens→Logits→Temperature Scaling→Softmax→Sampling→Autoregressive Loop

The prompt is first broken into tokens — the atomic units the model operates on. The transformer processes those tokens and produces a logit vector: one raw score per vocabulary entry. Temperature scaling adjusts the relative distances between those scores. Softmax converts the scaled scores into a probability distribution. A sampling strategy (greedy, Top-K, or Top-P) draws one token from that distribution. That token is appended to the context, and the entire process repeats for the next token. This pipeline is the unifying spine of this chapter and the conceptual prerequisite for everything that follows in this textbook.

The Question
If a language model has been trained on billions of documents that consistently describe Wonder Woman’s strength, why does changing temperature produce a different answer — and what does that reveal about the nature of every output an LLM produces?

What We Think Is Happening vs. What Is Actually Happening
Most people who interact with language models for the first time carry an intuition borrowed from search engines and databases: you ask a question, the system finds the answer, the answer is returned. This mental model is coherent, useful for many tools, and completely wrong when applied to transformers.

A database retrieves. A language model generates. The distinction is not semantic — it is architectural, and it has consequences that cascade through every application you will ever build with these systems.

To understand generation, you need to understand what the model has actually learned — and what it was trained to optimize. During training, a transformer processes an enormous corpus of text and adjusts billions of parameters according to a single objective: minimize the cross-entropy loss between the model’s predicted probability distribution and the actual next token in the training data. In plain terms, the model is rewarded for assigning high probability to whichever token actually came next in the training corpus, and penalized for spreading probability mass elsewhere. This is next-token prediction, and it is the only thing the training objective directly optimizes.

Notice what is absent from that objective: factual accuracy. The training process has no mechanism for checking whether the high-probability token is true — it checks only whether it matches the pattern in the training data. A sentence that confidently states an incorrect fact will receive a favorable training signal if that incorrect fact appeared frequently in the corpus. A sentence that hedges an accurate claim will receive a weaker signal. The model learns to generate plausible-sounding continuations, where plausibility is defined entirely by statistical patterns in text, not by correspondence to the world.

This is the mechanism behind the chapter’s most important corollary: high-confidence generation and factually correct generation are different things. A token that receives the highest logit in a given context is the token the model has learned to expect most frequently in that context. It is not the token that has been verified against ground truth. These two criteria often agree — high-frequency patterns in a large corpus tend to reflect accurate information about common facts. They diverge precisely in the cases that matter most: rare events, technical edge cases, and domains where authoritative sources were sparse in the training data.

A token is roughly a word, a subword fragment, or a punctuation mark — the atomic unit of language as the model experiences it. After training, what the model contains is not a filing cabinet of facts. It contains a learned conditional probability distribution: given everything written so far, how likely is each possible next token?

When you prompt the model, you are not unlocking a stored answer. You are seeding a probability distribution and asking the model to sample from it, one token at a time, until it reaches a stopping condition. The answer you receive is one draw from that distribution. Run the process again, and you may draw a different token at a critical branch point, which changes the subsequent context, which changes the next distribution, which produces a different sentence, a different paragraph, a different conclusion.

Every output is a path through a probability landscape. Temperature controls the shape of that landscape.

The Mathematics of the Next Token
To see precisely how this works, we need to examine what happens inside the model at the moment of generation.

The final layer of a transformer decoder produces a vector of raw scores — one score per token in the vocabulary. For a model using the GPT-2 tokenizer, the vocabulary contains approximately 50,257 tokens, so this vector has 50,257 components. These raw scores are called logits. A logit for token kk k can be thought of as the model’s unnormalized confidence that token kk k is the appropriate next element in the sequence.

Logits are not probabilities. They can be positive or negative, and they do not sum to one. To convert them into a probability distribution, the model applies the softmax function:

P(k)=ezk∑j=1VezjP(k) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j}}P(k)=∑j=1V​ezj​ezk​​

where zkz_k zk​ is the logit for token kk k and VV V is the vocabulary size. Softmax exponentiates every logit and normalizes by the sum of all exponentiated logits. The result is a proper probability distribution: every P(k)P(k) P(k) lies in (0,1)(0, 1) (0,1) and the values sum to exactly 1. The token with the highest logit receives the highest probability, but every token in the vocabulary receives some nonzero probability — even tokens that are grammatically absurd or contextually bizarre. The distribution assigns them negligible probability, not zero probability. That distinction matters.

Now temperature enters. Before the softmax is applied, each logit is divided by a scalar TT T, the temperature parameter:

P(k∣T)=ezk/T∑j=1Vezj/TP(k \mid T) = \frac{e^{z_k / T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j / T}}P(k∣T)=∑j=1V​ezj​/Tezk​/T​

This single division reshapes the entire probability landscape. When TT T is small — approaching zero — dividing by a small number amplifies the differences between logits. The highest logit becomes astronomically larger than its competitors after exponentiation, and the softmax output collapses toward a one-hot distribution: nearly all probability mass concentrates on the single most likely token. The model becomes deterministic in the limit. When TT T is large — significantly greater than 1 — dividing by a large number compresses the logit differences toward zero. After exponentiation, all tokens look nearly equally likely, and the softmax output flattens toward a uniform distribution. The model becomes entropic, unpredictable, willing to generate tokens that would otherwise receive vanishingly small probability.

To make this concrete: suppose a model assigns logits z1=5.0z_1 = 5.0 z1​=5.0 to the token “strength” and z2=3.0z_2 = 3.0 z2​=3.0 to the token “wisdom” as the next word in a sentence about Wonder Woman. At T=1T = 1 T=1, the softmax ratio of their probabilities is e5/e3=e2≈7.4e^5 / e^3 = e^2 \approx 7.4 e5/e3=e2≈7.4 — “strength” is about seven times more likely than “wisdom.” At T=0.5T = 0.5 T=0.5, the ratio becomes e10/e6=e4≈54.6e^{10} / e^6 = e^4 \approx 54.6 e10/e6=e4≈54.6 — “strength” is now fifty-four times more likely. At T=2.0T = 2.0 T=2.0, the ratio collapses to e2.5/e1.5=e1≈2.7e^{2.5} / e^{1.5} = e^1 \approx 2.7 e2.5/e1.5=e1≈2.7 — the gap between the two tokens has narrowed to a factor of less than three. The model that was strongly committed to “strength” at low temperature becomes genuinely uncertain between “strength” and “wisdom” at high temperature, and that uncertainty propagates through every subsequent token in the sequence.

The Wonder Woman experiment you ran at the beginning of this chapter was not an anecdote. It was a direct empirical observation of this mathematics.

Sampling Strategies: Navigating the Distribution
Knowing that the model produces a probability distribution over tokens does not fully specify how a token is chosen. Several strategies exist for drawing from that distribution, and they trade off coherence, diversity, and computational cost in ways that matter for practical applications.

Greedy decoding is the simplest strategy: always select the token with the highest probability. It is fast and deterministic but pathologically prone to repetition loops and degenerate outputs, because locally optimal choices at each step do not compose into globally coherent text. Greedy decoding is almost never used in production systems.

Top-K sampling restricts the sampling pool to the KK K highest-probability tokens before applying softmax normalization to that reduced set and sampling. Setting K=1K = 1 K=1 recovers greedy decoding; setting KK K equal to the full vocabulary size recovers unconstrained sampling. For intermediate values — K=40K = 40 K=40 or K=50K = 50 K=50 are common defaults — Top-K sampling excludes the long tail of improbable tokens while preserving meaningful diversity among plausible candidates. The weakness of Top-K is that KK K is a fixed count regardless of the shape of the distribution. In some contexts, the top 40 tokens all have non-trivial probability and truncation at 40 is reasonable. In others, one token has probability 0.95 and the next 39 together account for the remaining 0.05 — in this case, Top-K needlessly introduces variability from tokens that are contextually inappropriate.

Top-P sampling (also called nucleus sampling) addresses this by making the cutoff adaptive. Rather than truncating at a fixed count, Top-P retains the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold pp p. If p=0.9p = 0.9 p=0.9, the model retains however many tokens are needed to accumulate 90% of the probability mass — perhaps 3 tokens in a high-confidence context, perhaps 200 tokens in an ambiguous one. The sampling pool contracts and expands with the distribution’s entropy, keeping the model focused when confident and flexible when uncertain. This adaptive property is particularly evident in high-certainty contexts: after the fragment “The President of the United...”, the Top-P nucleus may contain a single token, because the cumulative probability threshold is met before any second candidate makes a meaningful contribution. After an open-ended creative prompt, the same threshold may not be reached until hundreds of tokens have been included. Top-P sampling is the default in most modern inference systems and is typically combined with a temperature setting rather than used in isolation.

These strategies are not interchangeable aesthetic choices. They encode assumptions about how you want the model to behave at the boundary of its uncertainty, and selecting them requires understanding what the model’s distribution looks like in the specific domain of your application.

How the Model Converges: Entropy Across Layers
The stochastic behavior visible at the output is the endpoint of a process that unfolds gradually across the transformer’s depth. Interpretability tools that decode intermediate layer activations back into vocabulary space — projecting the residual stream through the model’s own output head at each layer — reveal a consistent internal pattern: early layers expand, late layers prune.

In the early layers, the model entertains a broad field of candidate tokens, and the Shannon entropy of the intermediate distribution is high:

H(X)=−∑kP(k)log⁡P(k)H(X) = -\sum_{k} P(k) \log P(k) H(X)=−∑k​P(k)logP(k)

High entropy here is not indecision — it is the model accumulating contextual evidence before committing. As representations propagate through higher layers, probability mass consolidates onto a shrinking set of candidates. Entropy drops. The generation is converging. In well-trained models, this entropy collapse in the final layers is sharp and reliable for high-frequency patterns; it is gradual and incomplete for factual claims that are sparsely represented in the training data.

The practical consequence is that a model generating a response is often “on its way” to the correct answer but may not have sufficient architectural depth to fully resolve the distribution before the output layer forces a decision. Logit trajectory analysis — treating the score of a candidate token as a signal evolving across layers — can extrapolate whether a token is ascending toward dominance or plateauing in ambiguity. This layer-by-layer view of uncertainty is one reason that model depth and factual accuracy are correlated: more layers provide more opportunity for the pruning process to complete.

The Complication: Stochasticity Is Not Uniformly Distributed
The picture assembled so far — a model sampling from a probability distribution, with temperature and Top-P shaping the draw — is accurate, but it conceals a structural subtlety that becomes important the moment you try to reason about output reliability.

Stochasticity in a language model is not evenly distributed across the output. Some tokens are generated with near-certainty regardless of temperature because they are overwhelmingly constrained by grammar, common phrase patterns, or unambiguous factual context. The token following “The capital of France is” will be “Paris” or a close variant across an enormous range of temperatures, because the model’s logit for “Paris” in that context dwarfs every competitor by many orders of magnitude. Other tokens are generated under genuine distributional uncertainty — the model has learned that multiple continuations are plausible, contextually appropriate, and well-attested in the training data, so the logits are clustered and temperature has substantial leverage.

This means that two outputs from the same prompt at the same temperature can have very different internal structures of certainty. A factual claim embedded in a creative sentence may be generated with high confidence while the surrounding prose varies substantially across runs. Conversely, a sentence that looks fluent and authoritative may have been assembled through a sequence of low-confidence draws, each locally plausible, together producing a statement that is globally incoherent or factually incorrect.

You cannot inspect a model’s output and determine, from the text alone, which tokens were generated with high confidence and which were not. The model does not annotate its uncertainty in the surface string. This is not a design flaw that future models will correct — it is a structural consequence of generating text token by token from a probability distribution. The output is text. The uncertainty lives in the logit space that produced it, and that space is invisible to the reader.

This is why the mental model of “the model found the answer” is dangerous. The model generated a sequence. Whether that sequence corresponds to a retrievable fact, a plausible confabulation, or a creative synthesis is not determined by the surface features of the output.

Failure Case: The Confident Wrong Answer
The Wonder Woman experiment from this chapter’s opening is one instance of a failure class that traces directly to this mechanism. A second, less obvious instance involves not a single query but a chain of them.

In 2020, a financial services firm deployed an agentic system to automate the drafting of equity research summaries. The system retrieved recent filings, generated summaries of each, synthesized those summaries into a preliminary analyst note, and flagged passages for human review based on an internal confidence threshold. In production, reviewers began noticing that the system occasionally produced internally consistent but factually inverted conclusions — stating that revenue had increased when the retrieved filing reported a decline, or attributing a cost improvement to operational efficiency when the source document cited a one-time accounting adjustment. The summaries read fluently and passed the system’s own confidence filter, because the language of positive analyst notes is statistically coherent and well-represented in the training data regardless of the underlying numbers.

The failure had two components that compound each other. First, summarization is a generation task: the model produces a plausible continuation of the analyst-note register, not a verified extraction of figures. Second, the confidence filter was measuring distributional certainty — how strongly the model’s logit distribution favored the generated tokens — not factual accuracy. An output that is confidently wrong will clear a confidence threshold more reliably than an output that is uncertain and correct. The filter was screening for fluency while the reviewers were checking for truth, and those are different properties measured by different instruments.

The maximum-consequence point in this pipeline was not the final synthesis — it was the summarization step, where numerical claims in the source document were first translated into natural language. Error introduced at that step propagated forward as confident input to every subsequent generation, arriving at the human reviewer dressed in the syntactic clothing of a well-formed conclusion.

Several of those cases did not exist. The citations were fabricated — complete with plausible case names, docket numbers, and invented judicial holdings — by a language model the attorneys had used to assist in research. When opposing counsel attempted to retrieve the cited opinions, they found nothing. A federal judge sanctioned the attorneys. The firm faced significant professional and reputational consequences.

This failure is not mysterious once you understand the stochastic machine. A legal citation has the surface structure of a factual claim: it names a court, a year, parties, and a docket number. The model had been trained on vast quantities of legal text and had learned the distributional patterns of citation syntax extremely well. When asked to identify supporting precedents, the model did what it always does: it sampled from the probability distribution it had learned over legal language, conditioned on the task. It generated tokens that, one by one, were highly probable continuations of legal citation structure. It did not retrieve cases from a database. It never verified that the strings it generated corresponded to actual documents. Verification is not a capability the generation process contains.

The critical insight is that the model’s output was not a lie in any intentional sense. It was a draw from a distribution that assigned high probability to plausible-sounding legal citations. The model was doing exactly what it was built to do. The failure belongs to the practitioner who treated a probabilistic generation as a deterministic retrieval — who assumed that because the output looked like a fact, it was one.

Every application built on language model outputs must incorporate this lesson at the architectural level. The stochastic machine generates. Verification is a separate process that must be explicitly designed and explicitly executed.

Agentic Loops and the Problem of Propagating Uncertainty
The single-query case — one prompt, one response — is the simplest context in which stochastic generation operates. In agentic systems, where a language model generates outputs that become inputs to subsequent model calls, tool invocations, or downstream decisions, the stochastic nature of generation compounds.

Consider an agentic loop designed to automate literature review. The agent receives a research question, generates a set of search queries, retrieves documents based on those queries, generates summaries of retrieved documents, synthesizes those summaries into a preliminary findings statement, and flags claims that require human verification. At each step, the model is sampling from a distribution. An improbable token drawn at step one — an unusual word choice in a search query — may retrieve a different document set than the most probable query would have. That different document set conditions the summaries generated at step three, which conditions the synthesis at step four. By the time the agent produces a findings statement, the output reflects a path through a high-dimensional probability landscape that began with a single low-probability draw several steps earlier.

This propagation of stochasticity is not hypothetical. It is the expected behavior of any system where model outputs feed model inputs. The variance in the final output can be substantially larger than the variance of any individual generation step, because deviations compound rather than cancel.

One engineering response to this problem is confidence-based temperature adaptation: the agentic system monitors some proxy for the model’s output confidence — the entropy of the logit distribution, the margin between the top-two token probabilities, or an explicit self-evaluation step — and adjusts temperature downward when confidence falls below a threshold. More sophisticated implementations monitor token-level entropy in real time: when the model encounters new, potentially destabilizing information from an external tool call — a retrieved document that contradicts a prior step, a calculation result that falls outside the expected range — internal entropy spikes. The system detects this spike and triggers additional sampling branches before committing to a continuation, exploring more of the distribution before narrowing back toward a single path. The intuition is straightforward: when the model is uncertain, reduce the sampling entropy to force more conservative, reproducible outputs. When the model is confident, allow higher temperature to maintain diversity and avoid repetition traps.

This strategy has real merit but introduces its own complication. Confidence as measured by logit entropy is a property of the model’s internal distribution, not a reliable indicator of factual accuracy. A model can assign high confidence to a plausible confabulation — the legal citation case is precisely this — because the probability distribution over token sequences has no direct connection to ground truth. Confidence-based temperature adaptation reduces stochastic variance; it does not reduce the probability of generating a confident but incorrect output.

The human decision node in any agentic system must therefore be placed not at the point of maximum uncertainty, but at the point of maximum consequence. The agent can manage low-stakes variation autonomously. The student, engineer, or practitioner must intervene when the output will be acted upon, published, filed in court, or incorporated into a downstream system. Designing that intervention point is a human judgment the agent cannot substitute for.

Connections to System Design and Performance
The vocabulary of the stochastic machine — logits, softmax, temperature, Top-K, Top-P — is not abstract theory. It maps directly onto decisions that engineers make when building systems.

A customer service application that must produce consistent, policy-aligned responses across thousands of interactions will operate at low temperature with narrow Top-P, sacrificing diversity for reproducibility. A creative writing assistant that must generate novel, non-repetitive continuations will operate at higher temperature with broader Top-P, accepting increased variance in exchange for diversity. A medical information system that summarizes clinical literature will require not only constrained temperature settings but explicit retrieval augmentation — the model’s outputs will be grounded against verified documents at each step, because the cost of a confident confabulation in that domain is measured in patient harm rather than professional embarrassment.

These are not knob-twiddling decisions. They are architectural choices that follow from understanding what the model is doing and what failure looks like in the specific deployment context. The engineer who treats temperature as an aesthetic preference and Top-P as a default to be left unchanged is operating without a model of the system they are building.

Understanding the stochastic machine is the prerequisite for building anything on top of it. Chapters 2 and 3 return to the confidence≠accuracy problem in the context of prompt engineering — where prompt structure modulates the logit distribution before sampling even begins. Chapter 5 introduces retrieval-augmented generation as a direct architectural response to the training objective’s indifference to factual accuracy: by injecting verified source text into the context, RAG systems shift the distribution toward tokens that are grounded in documents rather than corpus patterns alone. Chapters 7 and 8 treat stochastic compounding across multi-agent pipelines as a system design constraint with its own failure modes and mitigation strategies. The pipeline introduced in this chapter — tokens → logits → temperature scaling → softmax → sampling → autoregressive loop — is the substrate all of those chapters operate on.

LLM Integration: Observing Your Own Generation
This chapter’s core claim — that LLMs sample from probability distributions rather than retrieve stored answers — is most viscerally understood through direct experimentation. The following activity is designed to use LLM tools to surface the model’s uncertainty in a way that remains invisible in ordinary interaction.

Using any model API that exposes token log-probabilities, submit the following prompt at temperature 1.0:

“The single most important factor in the French Revolution was”

Retrieve the top-5 token probabilities for the first generated token after the prompt. Record them. Then complete the generation and note the full output. Repeat this process five times without changing any parameters.

Your task is not to record what the model said. Your task is to build an explanatory account of why the distribution over that first token looked the way it did — what in the training data, the structure of the prompt, and the nature of historical attribution would produce that specific probability distribution. The LLM surfaces the data. The causal account is yours to construct.

The model cannot explain its own logit distribution. It can generate plausible-sounding explanations, and those explanations are themselves draws from a distribution, not verified introspective reports. Distinguishing between the model’s generated account of its own uncertainty and a principled external analysis of that uncertainty is precisely the higher-order thinking this activity requires.

Chapter Summary
A large language model does not retrieve answers. It generates them by sampling, one token at a time, from a learned conditional probability distribution over vocabulary. The logit vector produced by the final transformer layer is converted to a probability distribution via the softmax function, and temperature controls the concentration or dispersion of that distribution by scaling the logits before exponentiation. Top-K and Top-P sampling strategies determine how the model draws from the distribution once temperature has shaped it.

Every output is a path through a probability landscape. The path varies across runs because sampling is a stochastic process. The variation is not noise — it is the designed behavior of the system, and its magnitude is a direct function of the temperature parameter and the entropy of the model’s learned distribution in the relevant context.

Stochasticity is not uniformly distributed across a model’s outputs. Some tokens are generated with near-certainty; others are generated under genuine distributional uncertainty. The surface text does not reveal which is which. This invisibility of uncertainty is the root cause of the most consequential failures produced by deployed language model systems — of which the fabricated legal citations are a representative and well-documented example.

In agentic systems, stochasticity compounds across pipeline stages. Confidence-based temperature adaptation can reduce variance but cannot substitute for explicit human decision nodes placed at points of maximum consequence. The practitioner who understands the stochastic machine designs those nodes deliberately. The practitioner who does not discovers them in postmortem.

Chapter 1: End-of-Chapter Exercises
The Stochastic Machine: Probabilistic Generation in Language Models
A. Conceptual Foundation (10%)
The core insight of this chapter is that LLMs generate rather than retrieve. Every output is a path through a probability landscape shaped by logits, temperature, and sampling strategy. This has a direct consequence for how you prompt:

Low-stakes, well-defined questions → Direct prompts at low temperature work reliably

Complex reasoning or multi-step logic → Step-by-step prompts surface the model’s uncertainty before it compounds

Questions where the “right” framing is itself uncertain → Multi-LLM comparison reveals how prompt structure modulates the logit distribution before sampling begins

The exercises below are divided accordingly. For each exercise, the prompting strategy is labeled and justified.

B. Direct Calculation Problems (40%)
“Ask once, get your answer”

These problems have well-defined inputs and single correct outputs. The model’s logit distribution is sharply peaked in these contexts — temperature has little leverage, and elaborate prompting adds friction without benefit.

Exercise 1.1 — Softmax by Hand

Prompt type: Direct calculation

Given the following logit values for five tokens, calculate 
the softmax probability for each at temperature T=1.0:

Token A: z = 4.2  
Token B: z = 3.1  
Token C: z = 2.8  
Token D: z = 1.5  
Token E: z = 0.3

Show the final probability for each token rounded to 4 
decimal places. Which token dominates?
Why direct: Softmax is a closed-form formula with no ambiguity. One correct answer exists. The model should compute it cleanly without step-by-step scaffolding.

Exercise 1.2 — Temperature Probability Ratio

Prompt type: Direct calculation

Two tokens have logits z1 = 5.0 and z2 = 3.0.

Calculate the probability ratio P(z1)/P(z2) at each of 
the following temperatures: T = 0.5, T = 1.0, T = 2.0.

Use the formula: ratio = e^((z1-z2)/T)
Why direct: This is the exact numerical exercise from the chapter. The formula is explicit, the inputs are given, and the result is a single number per temperature. Verification is instant.

Exercise 1.3 — Top-P Nucleus Size

Prompt type: Direct calculation

A model produces the following probability distribution 
over its top tokens:

Token 1: 0.55  
Token 2: 0.20  
Token 3: 0.12  
Token 4: 0.07  
Token 5: 0.04  
Token 6: 0.02  

How many tokens are included in the Top-P nucleus 
at p = 0.90? At p = 0.95?
Why direct: Nucleus size is determined by cumulative sum — no ambiguity, no reasoning chain required.

Exercise 1.4 — Shannon Entropy

Prompt type: Direct calculation

Calculate the Shannon entropy H(X) for the following 
two probability distributions:

Distribution A: [0.97, 0.02, 0.01]  
Distribution B: [0.40, 0.35, 0.25]

Use H(X) = -Σ P(k) log₂ P(k)

Which distribution represents a model that is more 
certain about its next token? What does the entropy 
difference tell you about temperature's leverage in 
each case?
Why direct: Formula is given; calculation is mechanical. The interpretive question at the end is answerable from the number alone.

Exercise 1.5 — Top-K vs. Top-P Tradeoff

Prompt type: Direct calculation

A model's probability distribution has one token at 
0.92 and 49 remaining tokens sharing the remaining 0.08.

If Top-K = 50, how many tokens are in the sampling pool?  
If Top-P = 0.95, how many tokens are in the sampling pool?

Which strategy is more appropriate here, and why?
Why direct: The numbers are unambiguous. The “why” answer follows directly from the calculation — no exploration required.

C. Step-by-Step Reasoning Problems (30%)
“Show me your work”

These problems involve multi-step logic, error-prone reasoning chains, or conceptual relationships where understanding the process matters as much as reaching the answer. Prompt the model to externalize each step.

Exercise 1.6 — Deriving the Deterministic Threshold

Prompt type: Step-by-step reasoning

I want to understand when a language model transitions 
from genuinely stochastic to near-deterministic behavior.

Walk me through this step by step:

1. Start with the probability ratio formula: 
   ratio = e^(Δz / T), where Δz is the logit gap 
   between the top two tokens.

2. Solve algebraically for the value of T at which 
   this ratio equals exactly 2.0 (the point where 
   the runner-up is more than half as likely as 
   the leading token).

3. Interpret what this threshold means in plain 
   language for a practitioner choosing a temperature.

4. Give a concrete example: if Δz = 4.0, what is 
   the threshold temperature? What happens to 
   sampling behavior above and below it?

Show each algebraic step explicitly.
Why step-by-step: The algebra requires careful manipulation of logarithms. Skipping steps introduces sign errors. The interpretive steps (3 and 4) only make sense if steps 1 and 2 are verified.

Exercise 1.7 — Tracing a Confabulation

Prompt type: Step-by-step reasoning

A language model is asked: "What court case established 
the right to silence in the United States?"

It responds confidently: "Garner v. New Jersey (1958) 
established that defendants cannot be compelled to 
testify against themselves."

Walk me through why this output is plausible from 
the model's perspective even if factually incorrect:

Step 1: What patterns in legal training data would 
make "Garner v. New Jersey" a statistically plausible 
token sequence?

Step 2: Why would the surrounding legal language 
receive high logit scores regardless of factual accuracy?

Step 3: Why does the model's confidence (logit margin) 
tell us nothing about whether the citation is real?

Step 4: What single architectural addition would 
reduce the probability of this failure?

Explain each step before moving to the next.
Why step-by-step: This traces a causal chain from training objective → logit distribution → surface output → failure. Each link depends on the previous. A direct prompt would flatten the chain into a conclusion without exposing the mechanism.

Exercise 1.8 — Entropy Collapse Across Layers

Prompt type: Step-by-step reasoning

The chapter describes how entropy in a transformer 
decreases from early to late layers during generation.

Explain this process step by step:

1. What does high entropy in an early layer mean 
   about what the model is "considering"?

2. What is happening computationally as entropy 
   drops across deeper layers?

3. Why does this collapse happen more sharply for 
   high-frequency factual patterns than for rare 
   or technical claims?

4. How does this layer-by-layer view explain why 
   deeper models tend to be more factually reliable?

After each step, pause and check: does your explanation 
depend on anything from the previous step? If so, 
make that dependency explicit.
Why step-by-step: The relationship between entropy, depth, and accuracy is non-obvious. Students commonly conflate “more layers = more memory” with the actual mechanism. Forcing explicit dependency-tracking between steps catches this confusion.

Exercise 1.9 — Stochasticity Is Not Uniform

Prompt type: Step-by-step reasoning

Consider this sentence generated by a language model:

"The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis 
points in its March 2019 meeting, citing persistent 
inflationary pressure in the housing sector."

Some tokens in this sentence were generated with 
near-certainty. Others were generated under genuine 
distributional uncertainty.

Step by step:

1. Identify which tokens or phrases were almost 
   certainly high-confidence draws (near-deterministic 
   given context).

2. Identify which tokens or phrases were likely 
   low-confidence draws (multiple plausible alternatives 
   existed in the distribution).

3. Explain why the surface text provides no signal 
   about which tokens fell into which category.

4. What is the practical consequence of this invisibility 
   for someone who reads this sentence and treats it 
   as factual?
Why step-by-step: Students need to practice decomposing a fluent output into its token-level uncertainty structure — a skill that does not emerge from simply reading the chapter. The four steps build a habit of probabilistic reading.

D. Multi-LLM Comparison Problems (20–30%)
“Try multiple LLMs — what do you notice?”

These problems use disagreement between models as the primary learning signal. The goal is not to find the “right” answer — it is to understand how prompt structure, training data, and sampling interact to produce different distributions over the same question.

Exercise 1.10 — The Wonder Woman Replication

Multi-LLM comparison

Ask Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini the same prompt at their default settings:

"In one sentence, describe Wonder Woman's primary superpower."
Run each model three times without changing any settings. Record all nine outputs.

Compare:

How many distinct answers did each model produce across three runs?

Which model showed the most variation? The least?

Did any model produce a response that surprised you — one that foregrounded empathy, diplomacy, or inspiration rather than physical ability?

Do the models converge on the same superpower, or do they distribute probability across different framings?

Reflection prompt to run on any one model afterward:

"I just ran you three times on the same prompt about 
Wonder Woman's superpower and got different answers. 
Explain mechanically why that happened."
Evaluate the model’s explanation: does it accurately describe the logit/temperature mechanism, or does it generate a plausible-sounding but vague account? What does the quality of this self-explanation tell you about the limits of introspective generation?

Exercise 1.11 — Confidence vs. Accuracy

Multi-LLM comparison

Ask Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini:

"What is the Mata v. Avianca (2023) case, and what 
does it reveal about the reliability of language 
model outputs in professional contexts?"
Compare:

Do all three models get the core facts correct (fabricated citations, federal sanctions)?

Which model’s explanation best connects the failure to the underlying generation mechanism (logits, distribution, retrieval vs. generation)?

Does any model hedge or express uncertainty? Does any model state incorrect details confidently?

Which explanation would be most useful to show a non-technical professional who is about to use an LLM for legal research?

Reflection: A model that describes an LLM failure confidently but inaccurately is itself an instance of the failure it is describing. Did you observe this? If so, what does that tell you about using LLMs to evaluate LLM reliability?

Exercise 1.12 — Sampling Strategy Intuitions

Multi-LLM comparison

Ask Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini:

"A developer is building a medical information system 
that summarizes clinical literature for physicians. 
They need to choose temperature, Top-K or Top-P settings, 
and decide whether to add retrieval augmentation.

What sampling strategy would you recommend, and why? 
Be specific about parameter values and the failure 
modes each choice is designed to prevent."
Compare:

Do the models agree on low vs. high temperature for this use case?

Do they recommend Top-K, Top-P, or both? Do their justifications differ?

Which model most explicitly connects parameter choices to specific failure modes (confabulation, hallucination, overconfident wrong outputs)?

Does any model recommend retrieval augmentation without being asked? Is its justification sound?

Follow-up prompt (run on whichever model gave the weakest answer):

"You recommended [their setting]. What specific failure 
mode does that setting prevent? Give a concrete example 
of what a bad output would look like if you used the 
opposite setting instead."
Does the model’s follow-up response strengthen or weaken your confidence in its original recommendation?

E. Hands-On Exercises (10%)
Exercise 1.13 — Design Your Own Temperature Experiment

Without running code, design an experiment to empirically locate the deterministic threshold for a prompt of your choosing.

Specify: the prompt, the temperature values you would test, the metric you would use to measure diversity (the chapter uses type-token ratio — you may use this or propose an alternative), and the predicted shape of the diversity-vs-temperature curve based on the chapter’s mathematics.

Then run the experiment using any available LLM interface. Did the inflection point in your data match your prediction? If not, what does the discrepancy suggest about the logit gap for your chosen prompt?

Exercise 1.14 — Prompting Strategy Audit

Take any three prompts you have sent to an LLM in the past week. For each one, identify in retrospect which category it belonged to: direct calculation, step-by-step reasoning, or multi-LLM comparison. Was your original prompting strategy matched to the task? If not, rewrite the prompt using the appropriate strategy and compare the outputs. What changed?

caption
DNA repair pathways protect the genome from damage. Base excision repair removes single damaged bases, nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions caused by UV radiation, mismatch repair corrects replication errors, and double-strand break repair fixes complete breaks in both DNA strands. Defects in any of these pathways can lead to genomic instability and cancer development.

The intrinsic apoptotic pathway is initiated by cellular stress, which activates BH3-only proteins (Bid, Bim, Noxa, PUMA) that trigger Bax/Bak translocation to the outer mitochondrial membrane. Bax/Bak oligomerization forms a pore, releasing cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, where it binds Apaf-1 and ATP to assemble the apoptosome. The apoptosome activates caspase-9, which cleaves and activates executioner caspases-3 and -7 to execute apoptosis
